dublinCore.description: Compare continuous-time and discrete-time views of sinusoid, square wave, exponential and step signals while adjusting amplitude, frequency, phase, time shift and time scale, with closed-form energy, average power and RMS readouts.
relation: Chapter 2: Introduction to Signals and Systems

topic: Signal energy, average power and RMS
Time shifting, time scaling and time reversal
learningObjectives: Distinguish continuous-time and discrete-time representations of the same signal
Predict how amplitude, frequency and phase change a sinusoid
Classify a signal as an energy signal or a power signal from its energy and average power
Analyze how time shifting, time scaling and time reversal change a waveform and its energy or power
Explain why the samples of a sinusoid stop following the curve when f|a| exceeds 10 Hz

misconceptions.misconception: Shifting or scaling a signal changes its power
misconceptions.correction: A time shift never changes energy or power; scaling by a divides the energy of an energy signal by |a| and leaves the power of a power signal unchanged
misconceptions.evidence: Pin a sinusoid and move the time shift: the power readout does not change; set a = 2 on the exponential and its energy halves

misconceptions.misconception: A discrete-time signal is the continuous curve with the gaps left out, so its readouts always match
misconceptions.correction: x[n] exists only at integer n and its energy and power can differ from those of x(t)
misconceptions.evidence: At f = 10 Hz the sampled power reads 4.00 against 2.00 for the continuous curve, and the sampled exponential energy is about 20 times the continuous-time energy

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Plot of a sinusoid, square wave, decaying exponential or step function shown as a continuous-time curve and as discrete-time samples, with sliders for amplitude, frequency, phase, time shift and time scale, and a table of energy, average power and RMS amplitude.

controls.label: Signal
controls.description: Chooses the base signal: sinusoid, square wave, decaying exponential or step function

controls.label: View
controls.description: Shows the continuous-time curve, the discrete-time samples, or both

controls.label: Amplitude A
controls.description: Sets the amplitude A of the signal

controls.label: Frequency f (Hz) / decay rate alpha (1/s)
controls.description: Sets the frequency f of the sinusoid and square wave, or the decay rate alpha of the exponential; unused for the step

controls.label: Phase
controls.description: Sets the phase of the sinusoid and square wave; unused for the exponential and step

controls.label: Time shift t0
controls.description: Delays the signal by t0 seconds (negative values advance it)

controls.label: Time scale a
controls.description: Compresses (a > 1) or expands (a < 1) the signal in time

controls.label: Reverse
controls.description: Makes the time scale negative, which flips the signal about t = t0

controls.label: Pin
controls.description: Keeps the current signal on the plot for comparison; up to three signals can be pinned

visualElements.description: Amplitude versus time (or sample index) plot with a continuous curve and stems for the samples; pinned signals use different colors
Table of energy, average power, RMS amplitude and class for the continuous-time and discrete-time views, with a legend of the traces

model.description: Evaluates y(t) = x(a(t - t0)) for four basic signals, samples it every Ts = 0.05 s, and reports closed-form energy, average power and RMS amplitude for the ideal infinitely long signal

assumptions: Energy, power and RMS are closed-form values for the ideal, infinitely long signal
The discrete-time view uses a fixed sampling period of 0.05 s

instructionalStrategies: Predict-then-verify with the amplitude and time-scale sliders
Pin a signal and compare it with a shifted or scaled copy
extensions: Add the unit impulse and a user-drawn signal
Let the student change the sampling period Ts
